Naja naja.venom_type: Neurotoxic, with local tissue damage at the bite site
Naja naja.danger: Highly dangerous. One of India's 'Big Four' medically important snakes.
Naja naja.introduction: A well-known snake that spreads a wide hood when threatened. The hood often shows a spectacle-shaped mark on the back. Often seen near villages and farmland, where it hunts rodents.
Naja naja.range: India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh
Naja naja.habitat: Farmland, rice paddies, forest edges, scrubland, rock piles and areas near human settlements
Naja naja.diet: Rodents, frogs, toads, lizards, other snakes and bird eggs
Naja naja.length: About 1 to 1.5 m, occasionally up to about 2 m
Naja naja.activity: Mostly active at dusk and at night, but can be seen by day
Naja naja.how_to_recognise: Spreads a broad hood when alarmed. Colour ranges from brown to nearly black, and the hood usually has a spectacle mark.

Bungarus caeruleus.danger: Highly dangerous. One of the 'Big Four'. Bites can be nearly painless, so they may go unnoticed.
Bungarus caeruleus.introduction: A shy, nocturnal snake that is usually calm during the day but much more alert after dark. Bites often happen to people sleeping on the ground.
Bungarus caeruleus.range: India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh
Bungarus caeruleus.habitat: Plains, farmland, termite mounds, rodent burrows, and around houses and outbuildings
Bungarus caeruleus.diet: Other snakes (including other kraits), rodents, lizards and frogs
Bungarus caeruleus.length: About 0.9 to 1.2 m, occasionally up to about 1.75 m
Bungarus caeruleus.how_to_recognise: Glossy blue-black body with thin white crossbands (often clearer toward the rear), and a row of enlarged hexagonal scales along the back.

Daboia russelii.venom_type: Haemotoxic. Affects blood clotting and can damage the kidneys.
Daboia russelii.danger: Highly dangerous. One of the 'Big Four' and responsible for many snakebites in India.
Daboia russelii.introduction: A heavy-bodied viper that hisses loudly when disturbed. It is often found in open farmland and grassy areas, which brings it into contact with farm workers.
Daboia russelii.range: India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh
Daboia russelii.habitat: Open grassland, scrub, farmland, rice fields and rocky or bushy areas
Daboia russelii.diet: Rodents and other small mammals, lizards, frogs, birds, and large insects and scorpions (especially young snakes)
Daboia russelii.length: About 1 to 1.2 m, occasionally up to about 1.5 m
Daboia russelii.how_to_recognise: Stout body with a triangular head and a chain-like pattern of dark oval blotches ringed in white or yellow along the back.

Echis carinatus.venom_type: Haemotoxic. Affects blood clotting and can cause bleeding.
Echis carinatus.danger: Highly dangerous despite its small size. One of the 'Big Four'.
Echis carinatus.introduction: A small, irritable viper of dry country. When threatened it coils and rubs its keeled side scales together, making a rasping 'saw' sound as a warning.
Echis carinatus.range: Dry regions of India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, and nearby countries
Echis carinatus.habitat: Dry and sandy ground, semi-desert, scrub, rocky areas and farmland
Echis carinatus.diet: Small rodents, lizards, frogs, centipedes, scorpions and other arthropods
Echis carinatus.length: About 30 to 60 cm, occasionally up to about 80 cm
Echis carinatus.how_to_recognise: Small, sandy to brown snake with pale zigzag or spot markings along the sides, a rough keeled body, and a pale arrow or cross shape on the head.

Ptyas mucosa.danger: Harmless to humans, though it can bite and bites can hurt. Often mistaken for a cobra.
Ptyas mucosa.introduction: A large, fast and alert snake that is common around farms and villages. It is very useful to farmers because it eats large numbers of rodents.
Ptyas mucosa.range: India and much of South Asia, extending into Southeast Asia
Ptyas mucosa.habitat: Farmland, forests, scrub, villages, mangroves and areas near water
Ptyas mucosa.diet: Rodents, frogs, lizards, birds and other snakes
Ptyas mucosa.length: About 1.5 to 2 m, occasionally over 3 m
Ptyas mucosa.how_to_recognise: Long, slim body in brown, olive or yellowish tones, with dark crossbars toward the rear and large eyes. When threatened it may rise up and flatten its neck, which is why people confuse it with a cobra.

Fowlea piscator.venom_type: Not dangerous to humans (a mild, rear-fanged species)
Fowlea piscator.introduction: A common water snake of ponds, streams and flooded fields. It can flatten its neck and strike when frightened, which sometimes makes people think it is dangerous.
Fowlea piscator.range: Widespread across the Indian subcontinent and parts of Southeast Asia (the exact range depends on how species are classified)
Fowlea piscator.habitat: Ponds, lakes, streams, wetlands and paddy fields
Fowlea piscator.diet: Fish, frogs, tadpoles and toads, occasionally small rodents
Fowlea piscator.length: About 1 m, occasionally up to about 1.5 m
Fowlea piscator.how_to_recognise: Olive to brown body with a dark checkered pattern, dark stripes behind the eye, and keeled scales. Usually found near water.

Lycodon aulicus.danger: Harmless to humans. Frequently mistaken for a krait.
Lycodon aulicus.introduction: A small, fast, nocturnal snake that often enters houses and outbuildings hunting geckos. It gets its name from its enlarged, fang-like front teeth, which are used for gripping prey and are harmless to people.
Lycodon aulicus.range: India, Sri Lanka and nearby parts of South Asia
Lycodon aulicus.habitat: Houses, gardens, outbuildings, rocky areas and forest edges
Lycodon aulicus.diet: Geckos, skinks and other lizards, frogs and small rodents
Lycodon aulicus.how_to_recognise: Slim brown or dark body with narrow pale crossbands that are often most visible on the front half and may fade toward the tail. A broad head distinct from the neck.

Eryx johnii.introduction: A stout, burrowing snake of dry, sandy ground. Its blunt tail looks like its head, which has led to the myth of a 'two-headed snake'. This myth has driven illegal trade, and the species is legally protected in India.
Eryx johnii.range: India, Pakistan, Nepal and nearby dry regions
Eryx johnii.habitat: Dry, sandy or loose soil, semi-arid scrub and farmland, where it burrows
Eryx johnii.diet: Rodents and other small mammals, lizards and birds
Eryx johnii.activity: Nocturnal and crepuscular, spending much of the day buried
Eryx johnii.how_to_recognise: Thick, cylindrical body with smooth scales, a short blunt tail and a small head barely wider than the neck. Colour ranges from reddish brown to tan or dark brown.
